name: Silk Road
summary: Overland caravan corridor linking Han China to the Mediterranean via the Tarim Basin and Transoxiana. Carried silk west, and glass, horses, Buddhism and plague east.

name: Incense Route
summary: Caravan road carrying frankincense and myrrh from South Arabia to the Mediterranean. Made Petra and the Nabataeans rich.

name: Amber Road
summary: Baltic amber travelled south to the Adriatic and on to Rome, exchanged for bronze, wine and glass.

name: Trans-Saharan route
summary: Camel caravans crossed the Sahara carrying West African gold and salt north, funding Ghana, Mali and Songhai.

name: Varangians to the Greeks
summary: Norse river route from the Baltic down the Dnieper to Constantinople — the artery that made Kievan Rus'.

name: Grand Trunk Road
summary: South Asia's great east–west highway, laid out under the Mauryas and rebuilt by Sher Shah Suri and the British.

name: Cape Route to the Indies
summary: Portuguese sea road round the Cape of Good Hope to India and the spice islands — it broke the overland spice monopoly, and the Suez Canal ended it.

name: Atlantic crossing
summary: The Columbian route from Andalusia via the Canaries to the Caribbean, riding the trade winds west and the Gulf Stream home.

name: Tyre–Jerusalem road
summary: The overland link between Tyre, the leading Phoenician port, and Jerusalem in the Judean hills, drawn here down the coast to Akko, through the Jezreel Valley and along the hill-country ridge. In the biblical account Hiram of Tyre sent David and Solomon cedar, juniper and skilled builders, and Solomon paid in wheat and olive oil; the timber itself went mostly by sea, floated down the coast. These dealings are known from the Bible and from Tyrian records that Josephus quoted a thousand years later; the road is real geography, but its exact line is not known, so it is drawn schematically.

sources.use: the account; goods

sources.title: Ezekiel 27:17 (Judah and Israel trading wheat, honey, oil and balm with Tyre)

sources.title: Years
sources.use: from −1000: the account begins Tyre's dealings with Jerusalem under David (2 Samuel 5:11), conventionally c. 1000 BCE. To −586: Babylon's destruction of Jerusalem (587/586 BCE). The span covers the dealings the sources describe, not proof of continuous traffic.

sources.use: schematic: the stops are real Iron Age towns on the natural coast-to-hills corridor, but no source gives the road's exact line; the Hiram–Solomon dealings themselves rest on the biblical account and on Tyrian records known only through Josephus.

name: Red Sea voyages towards Ophir
summary: A sea lane from the head of the Gulf of Aqaba down the Red Sea, as told in the biblical account of Solomon's fleet: ships built at Ezion-Geber beside Elath, crewed partly by Hiram's Tyrian sailors, brought back gold, almug wood and precious stones from Ophir. Where Ophir lay is unknown (southern Arabia, the Horn of Africa and India have all been proposed), so the line stops in the southern Red Sea instead of at a claimed Ophir. Where Ezion-Geber stood is disputed too, and neither proposed site has yielded a tenth-century port, so the voyages are known only from the biblical text.

waypoints.name: Ezion-Geber (site disputed)
waypoints.note: The line starts in the water at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, where the account places Ezion-Geber. This point is not a claimed site; the candidates are listed.

candidates.name: Tell el-Kheleifeh
candidates.note: Proposed by Nelson Glueck, who dug it in 1938–40. Pratico's 1985 reappraisal dates its occupation to the 8th–early 6th centuries BCE and found nothing from the 10th; he left the identification open. Wikidata's Ezion-Geber item (Q1386052) uses this site's coordinates.

candidates.name: Jezirat Faraun (Pharaoh's Island)
candidates.note: Proposed by Alexander Flinder (1977, 1989) as the harbour, with Beno Rothenberg and Avner Raban arguing for the island too. Its earliest finds are Iron Age I pottery; the fortress standing today is medieval.

waypoints.name: Elath
waypoints.note: The account sets Ezion-Geber beside Elath (Eloth). Pleiades records Elath, and Ezion-Geber, as names of Aila at Aqaba; some scholars place Elath at Tell el-Kheleifeh instead.

waypoints.name: towards Ophir (location unknown)
waypoints.note: An open end in the southern Red Sea, not a place. Ophir's location is unknown; the account says only that the round trip brought gold. Proposed regions are listed without a pick.

candidates.name: Southern Arabia
candidates.note: Proposed: across the Red Sea from the Horn of Africa; the Bible lists Ophir among the peoples of Arabia (Genesis 10:29).

candidates.name: Horn of Africa / East Africa
candidates.note: Proposed: a gold-bearing coast reached down the Red Sea, sometimes linked with Egypt's land of Punt.

candidates.name: India
candidates.note: Proposed: from the goods named (almug wood, and in 1 Kings 10:22 ivory, apes and peacocks) and from Josephus, who placed Ophir in India (Antiquities 8.6.4).

sources.title: 1 Kings 9:26–28; 10:11 (the fleet at Ezion-Geber beside Eloth, Hiram's sailors, 420 talents of gold, almug wood and precious stones)
sources.use: the account; goods. 1 Kings 10:22's silver, ivory, apes and peacocks came with the 'ships of Tarshish', whose route is debated, so they are not listed as goods here.

sources.title: 2 Chronicles 8:17–18 (parallel account, 450 talents); 1 Kings 22:48 (Jehoshaphat's later fleet wrecked at Ezion-Geber)
sources.use: the account; why the route is not extended into the 9th century

sources.title: Gary D. Pratico, 'Nelson Glueck's 1938–1940 Excavations at Tell el-Kheleifeh: A Reappraisal', BASOR 259 (1985) 1–32
sources.use: Tell el-Kheleifeh's dates and the open identification (read through the hosted copy)

sources.title: Alexander Flinder, 'Is This Solomon's Seaport?', Biblical Archaeology Review 15:4 (1989)
sources.use: the Jezirat Faraun candidate (consulted through summaries, not read in full)

sources.title: 'A Shipment of Gold': the Tell Qasile ostracon, 8th century BCE, 'gold of Ophir to (or for) Beth-Horon, 30 shekels'
sources.use: Ophir as a known name for gold outside the Bible; the sherd does not locate Ophir

sources.title: Pleiades place records: Aelana/Aila 746700, Kheleifeh 746754
sources.use: place ids, coordinates, and Pleiades' own name records for Elath and Ezion-Geber (checked 2026-11-09)

sources.title: Wikidata: Pharaoh's Island Q933219, Straits of Tiran Q208157, Ezion-Geber Q1386052, Ophir Q914073; coastal towns Haql Q97291597, Nuweiba Q1011488, Dahab Q370495, Sharm el-Sheikh Q644
sources.use: ids and coordinates; the coastal towns were used to keep the line mid-gulf in the Gulf of Aqaba

sources.title: Years
sources.use: −970 to −931: the conventional dates of Solomon's reign, to which the account ties the voyages. They are not extended: Jehoshaphat's attempt in the 9th century failed (1 Kings 22:48), and the later Elath of 2 Kings 14:22 and 16:6 belongs to other stories.

sources.title: Certainty
sources.use: schematic: the line is drawn by hand down the only sea lane from the Gulf of Aqaba, and it stops short because Ophir is unknown. The voyages themselves are known only from the biblical text, written down centuries later, with no evidence from the time for the voyages, their port or their destination; this says nothing about whether they happened.

name: Cedar rafts, Tyre to Joppa
summary: The sea leg of the timber trade between Tyre and Jerusalem. In the Chronicles account, Hiram's men cut cedar and juniper in the Lebanon range, bound the logs into rafts and floated them down the coast to Joppa, where Solomon's workers took them over and hauled them up to Jerusalem for the temple; the parallel in 1 Kings names no port, and neither text says where the rafts set out, so the line starts at Tyre, Hiram's city. Shipping Lebanese timber along this coast is well documented in Egyptian texts, but this shipment is known only from the biblical account, and the line is drawn schematically a few kilometres offshore.

waypoints.name: Tyre
waypoints.note: Hiram's city. The accounts do not say where on the Lebanese coast the rafts were made up; Tyre stands in for that unnamed point.

waypoints.name: Dor
waypoints.note: A harbour the line passes; the accounts name no stops on the way.

waypoints.name: Joppa
waypoints.note: Where 2 Chronicles 2:16 lands the rafts; from here the timber went overland up to Jerusalem.

sources.title: 2 Chronicles 2:16 (timber from Lebanon floated by sea to Joppa, then carried up to Jerusalem)
sources.use: the account; the only text that names Joppa for Solomon's timber

sources.title: 1 Kings 5:8–9 (Hiram's men bring the timber down from Lebanon to the sea and float it in rafts to the place Solomon names)
sources.use: the parallel account; goods

sources.title: Ezra 3:7 (cedar brought by sea from Lebanon to Joppa for the Second Temple)
sources.use: a later use of the same sea lane (6th century BCE); not added to the years, since it is a separate episode

sources.title: The Report of Wenamun (Egypt, c. 1080 BCE): an Egyptian envoy sails to Byblos for cedar and calls at Dor on the way
sources.use: evidence from near the time that Lebanese timber went by sea along this coast; it does not concern Solomon's shipment

sources.use: place ids and coordinates of the waypoints and the coastal anchors (checked 2026-11-10); Pleiades attests Ioppe from its Egyptian–Hittite (Late Bronze Age) Levant period onward, so Joppa was an old harbour by the 10th century

sources.title: Years
sources.use: −970 to −931: the conventional dates of Solomon's reign, when both accounts set the timber deal with Hiram (the temple was built within it). The same as levant-red-sea, so a link at −950 shows both.

sources.title: Certainty
sources.use: schematic: the sea lane along this coast is certain geography and timber shipping on it is attested in Egyptian texts, but this shipment is known only from the biblical account (Chronicles, written down centuries later, is the only one to name Joppa), and the line is drawn approximately.
